newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa clothing industry pins hopes on U.S. mkt.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa clothing industry pins hopes on U.S. mkt.

text.p: The South African clothing and textile industry had entered a cautious recovery phase with its hopes mainly pinned on interest rate cuts and increased access to the U.S. market, it said on Friday.
"The industry appears to be moving into a cautious recovery phase," Clothing Federation of South Africa (Clofed) economist Paul Theron said in the latest issue of Clothing Industry News.

He and Investec Securities analyst Arnold Werbeloff said in separate articles in the newsletter that growth prospects were pinned on expected interest rate cuts, the benefits of a painful restructuring process filtering through to the industry at last and U.S. initiatives to increase trade with Africa.
Lower interest rates would boost consumer spending while restructuring would make the industry more competitive in export markets.

Werbeloff said that the U.S. government had appointed a commission to examine ways in which it could boost trade with reform-minded African countries, including quota-free and duty-free access by African clothing and textile firms to the U.S. market.
Clofed chairman Bernard Richards said a decision on this improved access was expected by September or October.
Werbeloff said that Africa supplied less than one percent or about $400 million of U.S. imports of clothing and textiles.
"The intention is to increase these products from the region to $3.5 billion per annum," Werbeloff said.
"Over the next eight years, that is until 2005, this would provide Africans with the potential to export goods worth $30 billion."
At the moment, only Kenya and Mauritius were significant suppliers to the U.S. market and the only countries facing quotas on their exports.

Werbeloff said that South Africa faced an average of 17 percent in duties on its clothing exports to the U.S. and in 1995 exported clothing worth 178 million rand to the U.S., or 36 percent of total exports of 490 million rand.
Textile exports were minimal at fibre worth four million rand, yarns worth seven million rand and fabrics worth seven million rand.

"If the duties on these products are abolished, we could face a major restructuring of the local clothing and textiles industries, with a significant influx of foreign players and a large boost to local production and exports," Werbeloff said.
"It would become vital in such a context for major local manufacturers either to have strategic alliances with foreign companies or to be held by these global competitors."
He said Clofed figures showed that about 3,000 South African clothing industry jobs depended on exports to the U.S. and another 26,000 jobs could be created if exports rose 10 times.

The companies most likely to benefit would be clothing manufacturer Seardel Investments Corporation Ltd, suit manufacturers Rex Trueform Clothing Company Ltd, Romatex Ltd subsidiary Hextex, Anglovaal Industries Ltd subsidiary S.A. Fine Worsted and Lenco Holdings Ltd .
